claims.text: The starting material is a mixed noble- and base-metal precursor deposited on TiO2.
Hydrogen spillover on TiO2 can generate strongly reducing hydrogen species that migrate rapidly from noble metals to adjacent base-metal precursors.
Spillover hydrogen species on TiO2 can reduce base metals at low temperature.
The relevant low-temperature synthesis regime is below 250 °C.
TiO2-assisted spillover causes noble- and base-metal precursors to reduce synchronously.
Synchronous reduction produces spatially uniform nucleation of mixed-metal clusters.
TiO2-assisted spillover enables alloy formation from noble/base-metal combinations that are immiscible at equilibrium.
The TiO2 spillover strategy can be applied to form TiO2-supported high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Coordinated precursor reduction suppresses phase segregation.
Coordinated precursor reduction suppresses differences in nucleation timing.
Suppression of segregation and nucleation delays yields a chemically homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
A well-mixed HEA nanoparticle structure creates more uniform catalytic active sites.
Uniform active sites produced by the well-mixed structure increase catalytic activity and stability.
TiO2-supported CoNiCuRuPd HEA nanoparticles can exhibit high activity and outstanding stability in CO2 hydrogenation.
Under otherwise similar low-temperature conditions, TiO2-supported catalysts will have a narrower compositional distribution than catalysts on inert supports.
Under otherwise similar low-temperature conditions, TiO2-supported catalysts will have higher catalytic activity and stability than catalysts on inert supports.
Direct low-temperature reduction on an inert support is expected to yield phase-separated or compositionally inhomogeneous particles.
At higher synthesis temperatures, thermal diffusion may dominate over the proposed spillover-controlled formation mechanism.
The proposed mechanism may not operate on supports that do not facilitate hydrogen spillover.
Metal loading, precursor chemistry, TiO2 morphology, nanoparticle size, and minor phases can affect the measured catalytic performance.
